title: Byte order
description:
A four-byte number can be stored lowest byte first (*little-endian*, as on your PC) or highest byte first (*big-endian*, the order network protocols use). Programs that read files or talk over a network have to convert.

Write, using only shifts and masks (no library byte-swap):

- `std::uint32_t swapBytes(std::uint32_t value)`: reverses the order of the four bytes, so `0x12345678` becomes `0x78563412`.
- `std::array<std::uint8_t, 4> toBigEndian(std::uint32_t value)`: the four bytes, most significant first, whatever machine the code runs on.
- `std::uint32_t fromBigEndian(const std::array<std::uint8_t, 4>& bytes)`: the reverse.

Because the last two are defined by arithmetic rather than by peeking at memory, they give the same answer on every computer.
rules: Use shifts and masks, not a library function.
lessonTitle: Memory Layout, Alignment, Unions and Bit Fields

rules.message: Use shifts and masks, not a library function.
